comment_body:
@ponharu This is a generated file from code in https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-dom-bindings/src/server/fizz-instruction-set/ReactDOMFizzInstructionSetShared.js using `yarn generate-inline-fizz-runtime` comand.

I hope this helps in getting this fix in

Thanks for pointing this out. I updated the source implementation in `ReactDOMFizzInstructionSetShared.js` and ran `yarn generate-inline-fizz-runtime` to verify the generated inline runtime is in sync.

The test makes it impossible to check if the leak is in React because the app code is leaking the signal itself. What is the real-world scenario that reproduces a memory leak? Is that still happening on the latest version on `main`?

Thanks — this is a fair concern. I think there are two separate things to distinguish here: what the React regression test is proving, and what the end-to-end reproduction is proving.

The test in this PR is intentionally a narrow regression test for the React invariant: the completion `cacheSignal()` abort reason should not capture a stack. It goes through the Flight completion path and verifies that the actual reason stored on `signal.reason` has no stack frames. It is not intended to be the leak reproducer by itself.

The real-world reproduction is the one from vercel/next.js#84648. The workload does not retain the `cacheSignal` from application code; it uses a dynamic server component with a slow upstream and clients disconnecting while the render is in progress. Under sustained high concurrency, retained heap grows after forced GC. The same workload was independently reproduced on Next 16.3.1 / 16.2.12 with React 19.2.8 and Node 24.

The strongest evidence there is the A/B with `--stack-trace-limit=0`: without the flag, retained heap after the load rounds was 407–2264 MB; with it, 68–157 MB. The two sets did not overlap, and the `stackTraceLimit=0` arm showed no accumulating trend across rounds. This is what led me to the React `new Error()` / captured CallSites retention path rather than application-level retention.

I also agree that suppressing the stack globally does not isolate this exact React call site, since it affects other stack-producing paths as well. That is why I'm treating the A/B as evidence that captured stacks are the dominant retained cost on this client-abort path, rather than as a proof that only this single `new Error()` is responsible.

For the second question, the issue is still reproducible on currently published React/Next versions; #84648 contains the recent independent reproductions. I can also run the shared repro against current React `main` to make that comparison explicit.

We can just abort with a string here and comment that we omit a stack because the stack isn't useful. The only useful part is the async stack ("which render completed?") which isn't available in this `error.stack`.
This can be removed. It's not about leaking but whether we want a stack and we want one by default. Only omitting the stack needs a reason.

Done in `0f283ae` -- both changes as you described them.

The completion site now aborts with the string, and the comment gives your reason rather than mine:
the only stack worth having here is the async one that says which render completed, and that is not
in `error.stack`. The `stackTraceLimit` helper is gone with it, so nothing touches process-wide state
any more. I also removed the leak-framed comment on the `fatalError` path -- you are right that a
stack is the default and only its absence needs explaining.

Two things worth flagging rather than leaving for CI to find.

**An existing assertion had to change.** `ReactCache-test.js` on `main` asserts
`renderedCacheSignal.reason.message`, which is `undefined` once the reason is a string. It now
asserts the reason itself. That assertion predates this PR and is the only place in the suite that
depended on this reason being an `Error`.

**Why a string is safe on the consuming path**, since an earlier review here argued for keeping the
`Error` type: the reason reaches `erroredTask` through `abortStream`, `abortIterable` and
`abortBlob`, and from there `emitErrorChunk`, which already branches on `error instanceof Error` and
for a plain value produces `String(error)` with an empty stack. So this is a shape that path already
supports.

I also dropped the stack-invariant test this PR had added. With a string there is no stack to assert,
and your earlier point about it stands regardless.

The description is updated to match.
